Introduction The beauty clinic sector in Indonesia is growing rapidly, yet faces significant hurdles in treatment cost transparency and initial diagnosis accuracy [1, 2]. This lack of clarity can confuse potential patients and undermine marketing efforts, especially in a competitive market where effective promotion is crucial [3]. Patients often hesitate due to unclear cost estimations, despite various appealing offers. Therefore, improving communication through clear and transparent cost estimations is vital for building trust and increasing market share [4]. Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based prediction models offer a promising solution. This study proposes using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) LangChain combined with Large Language Models (LLMs). This approach integrates data retrieval with natural language processing to generate accurate diagnostic predictions and efficient treatment cost estimations. By leveraging this model, beauty clinics can predict diagnoses from patient data, providing precise cost estimates and explanations. The tindakan table in MySQL provides the structured information necessary for exact service lookup and accurate cost estimation. The FAISS index is designed to be rebuildable locally on demand, allowing the system to easily adapt to updates or expansions of the clinic's knowledge base without requiring a complete system redeployment. 3.2. Discussion and Implications The RAG-LLM system for beauty clinic diagnosis and cost estimation significantly advances transparency and efficiency in Indonesia's beauty healthcare sector. Integrating structured (MySQL) and unstructured (FAISS) data with an intelligent LLM addresses critical challenges of initial diagnosis accuracy and cost transparency. This multimodal retrieval enables diagnostically relevant, financially transparent, and informative responses, enhancing patient trust and serving as a valuable data-driven marketing tool. The system's logic in recommending direct medical consultation for sensitive complaints is crucial for patient safety and responsible care. FAISS is vital for rapid semantic similarity searches on the unstructured knowledge base, ensuring highly contextual and relevant information enriches LLM prompts. This directly improves diagnostic accuracy and cost transparency by enabling more precise responses. Its rebuild capability ensures maintainability for knowledge base updates. However, system performance hinges on the quality and comprehensiveness of the MySQL knowledge table. Sparse or outdated entries limit contextual enrichment, affecting explanation quality. Keyword matching for search_layanan in MySQL may also miss relevant services if query phrasing varies, indicating a future area for improvement with advanced NLP.

text: Exploring a learning-to-rank approach to enhance the Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)-based electronic medical records search engines Cheng Ye * Department of Biomedical Informatics, Vanderbilt University Medical Center, Nashville, TN, USA A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Retrieval Augmented Generation Electronic medical records Information retrieval Large Language Model Learning to rank A B S T R A C T Background: This study addresses the challenge of enhancing Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) search engines for electronic medical records (EMR) by learning users’ distinct search semantics. The specific aim is to develop a learning-to-rank system that improves the accuracy and relevance of search results to support RAGbased search engines. Methods: Given a prompt or search query, the system first asks the user to label a few randomly selected documents, which contain some keywords, as relevant to the prompt or not. The system then identifies relevant sentences and adjusts word similarities by updating a medical semantic embedding. New documents are ranked by the number of relevant sentences identified by the weighted embedding. Only the top-ranked documents and sentences are provided to a Large-Language-Model (LLM) to generate answers for further review. Findings: To evaluate our approach, four medical researchers labeled documents based on their relevance to specific diseases. We measured the information retrieval performance of our approach and two baseline methods. Results show that our approach achieved at least a 0.60 Precision-at-10 (P @ 10) score with only ten positive labels, outperforming the baseline methods. In our pilot study, we demonstrate that the learned semantic preference can transfer to the analysis of unseen datasets, boosting the accuracy of an RAG model in extracting and explaining cancer progression diagnoses from 0.14 to 0.50. Interpretation: This study demonstrates that a customized learning-to-rank method can enhance state-of-the-art natural language models, such as LLMs, by quickly adapting to users’ semantics. This approach supports EMR document retrieval and helps RAG models generate clinically meaningful answers to specific questions, underscoring the potential of user-tailored learning-to-rank methods in clinical practice. Introduction Electronic medical records (EMRs) store diagnosis and treatment details and are, therefore, a potential resource for medical researchers.1–3 Unfortunately, scrolling through vast amounts of unstructured, redundant clinical text to identify relevant notes is time-consuming and expensive.4,5 EMR search engines are efficient tools to support information retrieval from EMRs.6–11 A technique named "learning-to-rank" was introduced to enhance EMR search engines. Learning-to-rank12,13 re-ranks search results by learning from labels provided by users. In general, a learning-to-rank approach represents each document by a set of features, such as bag-of-words. It then trains a classification model, such as a support vector machine or logistic regression, with user-provided labels to re-rank the search result.13,14 Learning-to-rank has been widely used in web search engines, such as Google,15 and recommendation systems in online retail, such as Amazon.16 In medical research, researchers also applied learning-to-rank approaches to identify important terms in a clinical document17,18 or to re-rank clinical documents to support medical research.19 Searching across medical records and producing labels is challenging because of an interesting paradox: even if a document contains a search term, a user may determine the document is not relevant to the search. For example, a note may reference "diabetes" in the past medical history, but the primary purpose of the note is a recent leg injury. While traditional learning-to-rank approaches can help focus the search on a user’s semantics, they can be limited because they require an offline training process and a large amount of training data, which is not suitable for one-time chart review tasks. As the state-of-the-art natural language model, the Large-LanguageModels (LLMs),20 such as the GPT-3.5 and GPT-4,21 Google’s Gemini,22 came to exist, one type of next-generation search engine, called Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)-based search engines, attract more and more attention, in both the artificial intelligence research field. An RAG-based search engine first retrieves relevant text segments from a target database based on the query or prompt provided by the users, and then the query and relevant text segments are provided to an LLM or multiple LLMs to generate answers to users’ query or prompt. A RAG-based search engine can efficiently overcome the hallucination issues when using the LLMs and can be a critical component of a reliable generative AI, especially for the application of generative AI in healthcare, which has specific legislations.23–26 Therefore, specific explorations of RAG-based search engines are needed better to shape the future research directions of next-generation generative AI and enhance the reliability and trustworthiness of the application of generative AI in healthcare. text: In this paper, we explore a novel learning-to-rank approach that learns to rank in the early stage (i.e., before sending search results to RAG-based LLMs) of chart review tasks with a limited number of positive labels. Given a clinical chart review task, as shown in Fig. 1, the system first extracts primary keywords from the clinical questions of the task identifies sentences in a document that are relevant to the keywords, and their expanded semantic similar words based on semantic models, such as word embeddings,27 medical semantic models.28 Then, we train a learning-to-rank model that learns to weigh the relevant sentences, which contain the keywords and their semantic similar words. The system learns to re-rank the relevant sentences and, therefore, refine the overall ranks of documents by re-computing the number of re-ranked positive sentences minus re-ranked negative sentences in the documents. After training a learning-to-rank model to adjust to the given clinical chart review task and the specific semantic needs of the users, the system moves to Step 2, as shown in Fig. 1. The system first transfers the clinical research questions into the pre-designed prompt template and then retrieves documents based on the recommendation of the trained learning-to-rank model. A selected Large Language Model (e.g., the GPT 3.5) receives the prompts and the refined document subset as the inputs and generates human-friendly answers. Such a hybrid approach that integrates the traditional learning-to-rank approach and the state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLM is able to generate explainable and reliable answers to support clinical chart reviews in a rapid and accurate manner. In this study, to evaluate the proposed learning-to-rank approach, we selected two finished clinical chart review tasks and extracted training and evaluation datasets from their action log files. In each of these two clinical chart review tasks, four medical researchers labeled a set of clinical documents based on a document’s relevance to the primary keywords of the clinical chart review tasks: "diabetes" or "seizure": (1) Clinical Chart review Task 1. These words surrounding the keywords can be used to infer the semantics of the search beyond a single search term. Our approach achieved high average P @ 10 scores across users with a limited number of positive-labeled documents, and the P @ 10 score further increased when more training data was added. This suggests the approach may be of particular benefit in the early stages of a chart review task when few labels are available. Our approach is able to learn and support users with a limited number of labels (e.g., in Table 1, user 3 only labeled 24 positive notes). As users provide more labels, the performance will continue to increase, as shown in Tables 4 and 6. For users looking to perform a single chart review, this approach can be used with minimal training requirements. The most difficult parts of utilizing limited positive samples (e.g., less than 10) are how to extract enough high-quality training data for a machine-learning model and how to generalize a learned model to unseen data. In our study, we introduced an assumption that a positive sentence always has a larger impact than a negative sentence. This assumption is necessary because (1) When given a new document with only one positive and one negative sentence, we always assume that a user is more likely to label it as a positive document; (2) It generates more effective training data to learn the impact values because we can consider all pairs of positive and negative sentences. For example, with ten positive sentences and ten negative sentences, we have 100 training samples. Similar to our assumption for building a training data set, the SVM-ranking13 method extracts users’ preferences from clickthrough data. Conclusion In this study, we proposed a learning-to-rank approach that quickly learns a user’s search semantics from a limited number of labeled documents. To demonstrate the generalizability of our approach, we selected a simple word embedding to help identify sentences and words that may impact a user’s decision and adjust the weights of words to learn a user’s search semantics. Moreover, our approach can be easily generalized to measure the impact values of unseen words using word embeddings or other semantic approaches (e.g., the BERT and BioBERT 30). The evaluation shows that, by learning the impact of words and sentences on the search term, our approach achieved better Precision at 10 (P @ 10) scores than baseline methods when only ten positive-labeled documents were provided. The learning-to-rank method may be used to support retrieving documents during a chart review with minimal training requirements and continues to improve its quality through active learning or be used as the foundation of a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)-based generative AI applied in healthcare industry. Introduction Radiology report generation is a critical component in the diagnostic and treatment processes of modern medicine. Radiology employs imaging modalities such as X-rays, CT scans, and MRI to visualize internal body structures for diagnostic and treatment purposes. The resulting reports serve as a vital bridge between raw imaging data and clinical decision-making [1]. A standard radiology report typically comprises two main sections: the Findings section, which provides an objective description of observations, and the Impression section, which offers clinical interpretation, summarizes key conclusions, and may recommend further diagnostic or therapeutic actions. Our study systematically evaluates similarity metrics for retrieval and the impact of negative sampling within the RAG pipeline. The approach extracts predicted findings and scores from a TorchXRayVision model, builds vector indices over MIMIC-CXR training reports, retrieves relevant neighbors using multiple strategies, and generates reports via a Large Language Model. In 16 controlled experiments, RAG consistently outperformed a non-retrieval baseline across both clinical (CheXbert and RadGraph) and linguistic (BERTScore, BLEU, METEOR, ROUGE-L) metrics. Moreover, adding explicit negative sampling at the prompt level consistently degrades performance, indicating that dissimilar reports confuse the LLM rather than provide useful guidance. Conceptually, RAG grounds a general-purpose LLM with precise, case-specific exemplars, steering it toward the specialized phrasing and clinical judgment of an expert radiologist. 826 Ghazal Zamaninejad et al. / Procedia Computer Science 275 (2026) 825–832 workloads, and the risk of interpretive variability. Given the high stakes, inaccuracies or ambiguities in these reports can significantly compromise patient care [2, 3]. Advances in artificial intelligence, particularly in natural language processing (NLP) and multimodal learning, have enabled automated systems to enhance the efficiency and precision of radiology report generation. Methods that jointly model images and text have proven especially effective in medical domains [4]. However, standalone generative models often suffer from hallucinations, inconsistent clinical style, and limited domain-specific expertise. Modern Large Language Models (LLMs), while powerful, behave as generalists—akin to a “general doctor” applying broad knowledge without case-specific exemplars—leading to generic or clinically inappropriate outputs. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses these shortcomings by incorporating relevant examples from external knowledge sources, yielding more accurate, factually grounded, and stylistically consistent outputs than purely generative approaches [5]. In radiology, RAG grounds the generator in historical reports from similar cases, supplying specialist-like examples and institutional phrasing that steer outputs toward accurate, clinically appropriate reports [6]. In this work, we integrate a visual predictor, named TorchXRayVision [7] with a retrieval component and an LLM generator (gpt-4o-mini [8]) to create a multimodal RAG framework tailored for chest X-ray report generation. Our primary contributions are: 1. Comprehensive analysis of retrieval strategies and similarity metrics: We evaluate Full vs. Partial Retrieval setups and compare four similarity metrics in the full-retrieval setting to maximize context relevance. 3. Empirical study of vector encodings and negative sampling: We systematically investigate two encoding schemes—non-binary probability vectors vs. binary thresholded vectors—and analyze the impact of explicit negative sampling (including dissimilar reports in the prompt) on generative quality. 2. Related Works Automated radiology report generation is a critical area in medical AI, aiming to reduce radiologist workload and improve patient care. A key challenge is the generation of incomplete or hallucinatory content, particularly references to non-existent prior studies, which are common in datasets like MIMIC-CXR [9]. To address this, preprocessing strategies like CXR-ReDonE [10] use GILBERT [11] a BioBERT-based [12] token classifier, to remove prior references, creating a refined dataset that enhances the performance of retrieval-based models like CXR-RePaiR [13]. Early methods approached report generation as image captioning, using CNN-RNN architectures, later evolving to Transformerbased encoder-decoder models [14, 15] and hybrid or graph-based approaches [16] to incorporate clinical knowledge, though challenges in ensuring report completeness and consistency persist. The emergence of large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) has advanced the field, with domain-specific models like CheXagent [17], designed for chest X-ray interpretation, and few-shot learners such as LLaVA-Med [18] and Med-Flamingo [19], optimized for biomedical visual question answering (VQA). Retrieval-Augmented Generation methods reduce hallucinations by grounding outputs in external knowledge bases. CXR-RePaiR [13], for example, reframes generation as a retrieval task, using CLIP [20] to rank image-report similarities, with sentence-level retrieval improving output relevance. Retrieval-Augmented Generation methods reduce hallucinations by grounding outputs in external knowledge bases. CXR-RePaiR [13], for example, reframes generation as a retrieval task, using CLIP [20] to rank image-report similarities, with sentence-level retrieval improving output relevance. Advanced RAG frameworks further refine this approach: LaB-RAG [6] employs categorical labels as natural language descriptors, derived from logistic classifiers on frozen image embeddings (e.g., BioViL-T [21]), to enhance retrieval through label-based filtering and prompt integration for in-context learning, achieving performance comparable to supervised fine-tuning methods like CheXagent and CXR-Mate [22]. Similarly, MMed-RAG [23], a multimodal RAG system, improves factual accuracy across medical domains like radiology by using domain-aware retrieval, adaptive context selection to filter irrelevant documents, and preference fine-tuning to address cross-modality and overall alignment issues, enhancing report generation quality. To align with radiologist workflows, models like CXR-Mate incorporate multi-view images and longitudinal data from prior reports, using LoRA adaptations and section embeddings to improve diagnostic accuracy, even when prior studies are unavailable [22]. Recent advancements introduce AI agents for tool orchestration, such as MedRAX [24], a specialized framework for chest X-ray interpretation. MedRAX employs a ReAct loop with LLMs like GPT-4o to integrate tools for report generation (using SwinV2), Ghazal Zamaninejad et al. / Procedia Computer Science 275 (2026) 825–832 827 classification (DenseNet-121), grounding (Maira-2 [25]), and VQA (CheXagent, LLaVA-Med), improving complex reasoning compared to end-to-end models. 3. Methodology This section describes the multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline we use for chest X-ray report generation. We first outline the overall design and then provide a formal description of the indexing and retrieval operations, the two vector representation schemes (non-binary vs. binary), the similarity metrics evaluated, the retrieval modes, and the negative-sampling strategy. 3.1. Overview Our objective is to generate clinically accurate FINDINGS and IMPRESSION sections for chest X-rays by combining (1) structured visual predictions from a radiology image model and (2) case-relevant textual exemplars retrieved from a large corpus of reports. Overview Our objective is to generate clinically accurate FINDINGS and IMPRESSION sections for chest X-rays by combining (1) structured visual predictions from a radiology image model and (2) case-relevant textual exemplars retrieved from a large corpus of reports. The design is driven by two hypotheses: (i) retrieval of exemplar reports supplies stylistic and co-occurrence priors that reduce hallucinations and improve phrasing, and (ii) the way we represent visual outputs (continuous probabilities vs. thresholded binaries) and the similarity metric used for retrieval materially affects which exemplars are returned and therefore the final generation quality. The complete pipeline is shown in Fig. 1 and consists of three stages: 1. Image-to-vector extraction via TorchXRayVision 2. Retrieval over an indexed corpus of training reports 3. Conditioned generation with gpt-4o-mini We evaluate multiple variants of stage (2) while keeping (1) and (3) fixed to isolate the effects of vector encoding, distance metric, retrieval granularity, and negative-sampling. TorchXRayVision outputs a 14-dimensional probability vector per view, corresponding to the standard CheXbert pathologies. After aligning with the textual labels present in the MIMIC-CXR reports and excluding dataset-specific or unsupported classes, 11 pathologies remain fully overlapping. We aggregate view-level outputs into a single study vector using mean pooling: ps = 1 m m v=1 p(v). We also construct a binary variant by thresholding: bs[i] = 1{ps[i] ≥τ}, where τ is a chosen threshold. Define the retrieval corpus (index) as D = {(xj, rj)}N j=1, where xj is the stored vector for training study j (either pj or bj) and rj is the textual report. Given a query study s with query vector xq, we compute a similarity score sim(xq, x j) for every j and return the top-K reports ranked by similarity. The end-to-end process for a single test study s is summarized below in pseudo-code 1: Algorithm 1: Multi-View Retrieval-Augmented Report Generation Input :study images, index D, similarity metric sim, threshold τ, retrieval mode, K, T, Kneg Extract per-view probabilities {p(v)}m v=1 ps ←1 m v p(v) if binary mode then bs ←1{ps ≥τ} xq ←bs end else xq ←ps end if Full retrieval then Compute sim(xq, xj) for all j and return top-K reports end else Select top-T indices of ps Perform per-label masked retrieval, return aggregated set of up to K reports end Optionally add Kneg farthest reports as negative exemplars Construct user prompt with predicted findings (with/without scores), positive similar samples (and negatives) Call LLM to generate FINDINGS and IMPRESSION 3.4. Similarity metrics We evaluate four common metrics for measuring proximity between study vectors: Cosine, Euclidean, Jaccard, and Hamming. Cosine similarity emphasizes the direction of the feature vectors rather than their magnitude, making it suitable when the relative pattern of findings is more informative than their absolute probabilities. Euclidean distance captures overall geometric closeness in the feature space, rewarding cases with similar probability magnitudes across all labels. Jaccard similarity focuses on the overlap of activated findings and is therefore effective for binary representations that describe presence or absence of conditions. Finally, Hamming similarity measures

Euclidean distance captures overall geometric closeness in the feature space, rewarding cases with similar probability magnitudes across all labels. Jaccard similarity focuses on the overlap of activated findings and is therefore effective for binary representations that describe presence or absence of conditions. Finally, Hamming similarity measures how many individual label predictions match between two studies, which helps identify reports with nearly identical binary finding profiles. This choice deliberately spans the most common geometric assumptions in medical retrieval: Cosine and Euclidean respect probability magnitudes and diagnostic confidence in continuous space, whereas Jaccard and Hamming enforce Ghazal Zamaninejad et al. / Procedia Computer Science 275 (2026) 825–832 829 strict binary agreement on presence/absence of findings—allowing us to determine whether preserving rich probabilistic information or collapsing it to binary labels better drives clinically accurate and fluent report generation. 3.5. Retrieval modes We compare two complementary retrieval granularities to examine the classic global-vs-local trade-off in medical exemplar selection: Full retrieval. Compute similarity between the full study vector xq and every x j ∈D, and return the top-K reports {r(1), . . . , r(K)}. This mode retrieves examples that are globally similar across the full label set, favoring studies that match overall disease co-occurrence patterns. Partial (per-finding) retrieval. Identify the top-T labels by descending probability in ps. For each selected label index i, perform a masked retrieval that focuses on that label. Aggregate the per-label neighbors into a short exemplar set. This mode emphasizes fine-grained exemplars for the most likely findings. Both modes are evaluated to determine which strategy better supports clinically accurate and linguistically fluent report generation. 3.6. Negative-sampling design To study negative guidance, we construct prompt contexts that contain: • Kpos positive exemplars (top-K similar reports), and • Kneg negative exemplars (the most dissimilar reports by the chosen similarity metric). Negative examples are explicitly labeled in the prompt as “negative” and instructions state that the model should avoid making the errors illustrated by these negative exemplars. This is a prompt-level test of negative sampling (distinct from contrastive training).

Prompt design Our framework uses two levels of prompting: a fixed system prompt that defines the model’s role and behavior, and a dynamically generated user prompt that provides case-specific input. The system prompt instructs the LLM to act as a board-certified radiologist and to produce only the FINDINGS and IMPRESSION sections. We design four variants of the system prompt to match the experimental configurations: 1. A baseline version that relies solely on TXR-predicted labels without any retrieved reports 2. A standard RAG version that instructs the model to also use retrieved reports as additional context 3. A partial-retrieval version that highlights using reports retrieved for each individual finding along with TXR labels 4. A version used in experiments with both similar and dissimilar reports, where the model is told to use similar reports for guidance and negative (dissimilar) ones only to avoid incorrect inferences The user prompt is generated dynamically for each study and contains the predicted findings (with or without their probability scores) and the retrieved positive or negative reports depending on the experimental setup. Retrieval mode: Full retrieval achieves the best overall clinical accuracy, while partial retrieval can enhance detailed description of top findings but may miss less probable conditions. 6. Conclusion We presented a systematic study of retrieval strategies for radiology report generation, analyzing the impact of similarity metrics, vector encodings, and negative sampling. Our experiments demonstrate that Retrieval-Augmented Generation significantly improves clinical accuracy and linguistic quality by grounding a generalist LLM with relevant exemplar reports—helping it behave more like a specialist radiologist. Among all tested configurations, non-binary probability vectors combined with Euclidean or Cosine similarity in Full Retrieval yielded the best clinical results. Binary encodings can be sufficient for lightweight retrieval but lose subtle probability information crucial for clinical phrasing. Moreover, na¨ıve prompt-level negative sampling consistently reduces performance, confirming that simply including dissimilar reports in the prompt confuses the LLM rather than guiding it.

text: Original Research Optimising clinical information extraction: a comparative study of retrieval-augmented generation techniques in clinical notes Hengyi Zhang a, Dinithi Vithanage a, Chao Deng b , Ping Yu a,* a Centre for Digital Transformation, School of Computing and Information Technology, University of Wollongong, Wollongong, Australia b School of Medical, Indigenous and Health Sciences, University of Wollongong, Wollongong, Australia A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Retrieval-augmented generation Information extraction Named entity recognition Large language model Dense retrieval Sparse retrieval Clinical notes A B S T R A C T Extracting clinically meaningful information from free-text notes in specific clinical settings, such as Australian aged care facilities, remains challenging due to the heterogeneity of text documents, which lack standardised structure and terminology. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can improve the precision and grounding of large language model (LLM) outputs; however, the choice of retrieval strategies remains understudied despite its critical importance for clinical information extraction (IE). Using real-world clinical notes from Australian aged care facilities, we systematically compare six retrieval methods within a unified RAG pipeline: sparse retrieval (BM25), dense retrieval (bi-encoder embeddings), dense retrieval with cross-encoder rerank (abbreviated as dense reranking), dynamic linear fusion of sparse and dense scores, reciprocal rank fusion (RRF), and hybrid coarse-to-fine reranking. We evaluate these strategies on two clinical named entity recognition tasks, extracting agitation symptoms in dementia (n = 208) and identifying malnutrition risk factors (n = 208) across five di­ mensions: context relevance, answer quality, source faithfulness, contextual diversity, and item-level accuracy. A repeated-measures ANOVA reveals that reranking and hybrid ensemble strategies significantly outperform both standalone sparse (BM25) and dense retrieval across both tasks. For agitation extraction, Dense reranking ach­ ieves the highest Answer F1 (0.946), Context Diversity (0.895) and Item-level Accuracy (0.963). For malnutri­ tion, ensemble methods yield the best Item-level Accuracy (0.944), followed closely by dense reranking. Through error analysis, we identify three LLM error types in clinical named entity recognition: intrinsic hallucination, extrinsic hallucination, and false negatives, and elucidate how RAG mitigates each. Introduction Due to a lack of standardised terminology and structure in nursing documentation in Australian residential aged care settings, the major clinical information is locked in free-text clinical notes. These notes are highly heterogeneous, characterised by varying writing styles and lan­ guages across staff [1], inconsistent terminology and structure across facilities [2], frequent abbreviations, context-dependent acronyms, and typographical errors. Extracting essential clinical variables from such unstructured text is therefore a significant challenge, one that clinical named entity recognition (NER) methods in natural language processing are well positioned to address [3]. Large language models (LLMs) offer powerful capabilities for extracting structured information from unstructured clinical notes. However, foundation LLMs that lack domain-specific pretraining can produce inaccurate, hallucinated, or biased outputs [4], raising concerns about their deployment in high-stakes healthcare contexts, where pre­ cision, contextual understanding, and domain-specific knowledge are paramount [5]. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) addresses these limitations by incorporating external evidence into the generation pro­ cess, enabling more accurate and contextually grounded clinical infor­ mation extraction [5,6]. The RAG framework integrates two core processes, retrieval and generation [7]. During retrieval, a knowledge source, which may consist of external documents, clinical guidelines, or clinical records [6], is pre- coded by a document encoder into dense vector representations. These vector embeddings are stored in a vector database for efficient similarity-based retrieval [7,8]. When a user submits a query, the retrieval module identifies the top-k most relevant documents through vector similarity matching, providing the LLM with dynamically accessed, pertinent context [9]. In the subsequent generation stage, both the original query and the retrieved documents are passed to a pre- trained decoder model such as GPT or Llama [6]. This model uses the retrieved content as external context to produce more relevant, factually grounded responses. The relevance and specificity of the retrieved documents directly influence the accuracy of downstream outputs; irrelevant or low-quality retrievals can lead to erroneous, incomplete, or misleading generated content. Consequently, selecting and optimising the retrieval strategy is critical for producing clinically meaningful and trustworthy LLM outputs aligned with user intent. Various retrieval approaches have been developed, ranging from sparse lexical matching (e.g., BM25) to dense neural embeddings and hybrid ensemble methods. However, their comparative effectiveness for clinical information extraction tasks, particularly in specialised settings such as Australian residential aged care, remains understudied. To address this gap, we systematically evaluate six retrieval strate­ gies within a unified RAG pipeline for clinical named entity recognition using real-world clinical notes from Australian residential aged care facilities. We assess performance across two clinically significant tasks: extracting agitation symptoms in dementia and identifying malnutrition risk factors, and evaluate five dimensions: context relevance, answer quality, source faithfulness, contextual diversity, and item-level accu­ racy. Assessing linguistic diversity of clinical notes Clinical notes express the same clinical concept through many different surface forms, directly affecting RAC retrieval performance. However, surface vocabulary breadth may overestimate the true diversity of clinical content if the semantic layer is not independently assessed. Sohn et al. [12] demonstrated that while the lexicon of clinical notes shows considerable variability across institutions, the overall se­ mantics remains highly similar at the conceptual level. Therefore, assessing linguistic diversity requires capturing lexical and semantic dimensions independently. Jarvis [13] identifies vari­ ability (the range of different word types) and disparity (the degree to which these word types differ semantically) as separable dimensions of text diversity, each requiring independent measurement [14]. Following this framework, we assess the linguistic diversity of clinical notes using two complementary measures: lexical diversity and intra-content se­ mantic dispersion. First, lexical diversity is computed as the type–token ratio, i.e., the ratio of unique word types to total tokens, to capture surface-level vo­ cabulary variation [15]. Let R = {r1, r2, …, rk} denote the set of text segments in a clinical corpus, V(R) the set of unique tokens after toke­ nisation, and T(R) the total token count. Lexical diversity (LD) is defined as: Lexical Diversity(LD) = |V(R)| T(R) Second, intra-content semantic dispersion is computed as the mean pairwise cosine distance between document-level term-frequency vec­ tors, capturing whether documents occupy distinct regions of the distributional semantic space or cluster around similar content. Concordance between the two measures indicates that vocabulary breadth reflects genuine content heterogeneity, whereas discordance suggests that substantial lexical variation conceals largely repetitive concepts. This diagnostic assessment provides essential context for interpreting the retrieval comparisons reported in subsequent sections. 2.2. The six strategies include (R1) sparse lexical retrieval (BM25), (R2) dense bi-encoder retrieval, (R3) two-stage dense reranking with a cross-encoder, (R4) dynamic linear fusion of sparse and dense scores, (R5) reciprocal rank fusion (RRF), and (R6) hybrid BM25 to dense rerank (coarse-to-fine). R1: Sparse Retrieval (BM25) Sparse retrieval (BM25) is a classical retrieval method. It ranks documents by term frequency-inverse document frequency TF-IDF ranking and probabilistic term weighting [17]. It uses lexical match­ ing to identify relevant documents, assuming that the frequency and distribution of exact terms can reflect relevance. This method uses the BM25 API to score each document against the tokenised query using two tunable parameters: k for term frequency saturation and b for document length normalisation. The top-3 highest-scoring documents are concat­ enated to form the context, which is then passed to an LLM for gener­ ation. In domains such as structured clinical narratives, where terminology is stable, and cues recur in consistent lexical forms, this method works well. It is interpretable, fast, transparent, and easy to scale [16,17]. However, clinical text can be messy, containing abbre­ viations, paraphrases, and local shorthand. R3: Dense Retrieval with Cross-encoder Reranking (Dense Reranking) Dense retrieval with cross-encoder reranking excels at capturing broad semantic relationships by independently encoding the query and document, enabling flexible matching across diverse contexts [25,26]. It adopts a coarse-to-fine strategy that balances retrieval breadth with ranking depth. A Sentence Transformer bi-encoder first proposes the top-10 candidates by cosine similarity; a transformer cross-encoder then reranks these candidates, and the top-3 proceed to the LLM for gener­ ation [27,28]. The final cross-encoder reranking step incorporates query-document interactions, yielding context-sensitive precision gains over bi-encoder retrieval [26,28]. The result is a balanced, broad se­ mantic recall, followed by precise, context-aware scoring. It is thus well- suited to healthcare, where small textual cues can flip clinical meaning [29]. Its main limitation is computational cost. Cross-encoder inference is slower and more challenging to scale than bi-encoder models, demanding batching, parallelisation, or distillation to meet real-time constraints [30]. R4: Dynamic Linear Fusion of Sparse and Dense Retrieval Rather than choosing between lexical and semantic signals, dynamic linear fusion retrieval lets the query decide which to use. It linearly fuses BM25 scores with dense cosine similarities after per-query min–max normalisation. It uses the dispersion of each score distribution (e.g., the standard deviation) as a proxy for its discriminative power on that query and weights the fusion accordingly; the top-3 fused results are passed to the LLM [28,31]. Methods This study systematically evaluates six retrieval strategies within a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline for an LLM to extract clinical information from clinical notes. The information retrieval task is named-entity recognition for two health conditions that older people in residential aged care facilities commonly experience: (1) symptoms of agitation in dementia, and (2) malnutrition risk factors. We rigorously evaluated the retrieval strategies in the RAG framework across five performance dimensions. 3.1. Ethics considerations This study was approved by the University of Wollongong Human Research Ethics Committee (Reference No.: 2019/159). The de- identified clinical dataset was nursing progress notes gathered from 40 residential aged care facilities in New South Wales, Australia, between 2019 and 2021. The research process consists of two phases: data preparation, a four- stage RAG-LLM pipeline, and model evaluation. 3.2. First, clinical IE tasks are normalisation- oriented: the model must not only locate relevant mentions but also map them to canonical concepts in a controlled schema (e.g., mapping “won't eat” to poor appetite in the malnutrition ontology). Second, clinical IE tasks are aggregative: a single nursing note may contain multiple extractable entities, requiring the retrieval system to surface passages covering diverse aspects of the note rather than converging on a single best answer. These two properties mean that retrieval errors in clinical IE compound differently than in open-domain question answering: they affect not only answer correctness but also the completeness and internal consistency of the structured output. Error Structure in Clinical Information Extraction versus General- domain Retrieval In the clinical IE setting examined here, intrinsic fabrications were the most prevalent error type, as found in other settings [42]. This pattern aligns with the imperfect representation learning and erroneous decoding mechanisms identified by Ji et al. as contributors to intrinsic hallucination: encoders can learn wrong correlations between different parts of the input, and decoders can attend to the wrong part of the source, generating outputs that mix facts between two similar entities [42]. It is also consistent with the normalisation demands of clinical IE: when the extraction schema requires a canonical term and the source text uses an informal or ambiguous expression, the model is more likely to mis-normalise (intrinsic fabrication) than to invent an entity from nothing (extrinsic fabrication). Extrinsic fabrications, though less frequent, arise from three mech­ anisms that are well-documented in hallucination literature: (1) para­ metric knowledge bias, retrieval-generation conflict, when the retrieved document contradicts the model’s parametric knowledge, causing the model to struggle to reconcile the two, sometimes defaulting to its in­ ternal and potentially outdated knowledge [63]; (2) long-tail knowledge gaps: LLMs perform well on common clinical concepts but are prone to fabrication when encountering rare or facility-specific entities (e.g., non-standard wound grading scales) that are underrepresented in training data; and (3) schema-driven over-completion: in the normalization-oriented extraction tasks examined here, the extraction schema itself can inadvertently elicit extrinsic fabrications [64] when the source text lacks information for

Limitations We acknowledge the following study limitations. First, this study evaluated only two clinical IE tasks: agitation symptoms in dementia (83 entities) and malnutrition risk factors (37 entities). Both are normalisation-oriented named entity recognition tasks operating on aged care nursing notes. While the results were largely consistent across these two tasks, they differ in ways that partially address concerns about task dependence: the agitation schema involves substantially greater terminological variability and a larger entity set than the malnutrition schema, and the two tasks produce queries of differing complexity and specificity. The stability of retrieval strategy rankings across these contrasting conditions provides some evidence of robustness. Never­ theless, two tasks are insufficient to support broadly generalisable conclusions about retrieval strategy performance across the full range of clinical IE scenarios. In particular, this study did not evaluate tasks involving relation extraction, temporal reasoning, or open-ended clinical question answering, each of which would impose different demands on the retrieval component in terms of query structure, required context length, and the degree of cross-passage reasoning. Furthermore, the queries in both tasks are schema-driven, i.e., they are structured around a predefined entity list rather than formulated as free-form clinical questions, and retrieval performance is known to depend heavily on query complexity, specificity, and structure. The findings should therefore be interpreted as evidence of retrieval strategy behaviour within schema-driven clinical NER, rather than as generalisable claims about retrieval performance across arbitrary clinical question types. Retrieval module The retrieval component is responsible for fetching relevant sentence pairs from the domain-specific parallel corpus to support the generation module in producing more accurate translations. It comprises two main components: a sentence embedding module and a vector database. 3.2.1 Vector Database For similarity-based retrieval, used FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search) [22], an open-source library optimized for high-speed vector similarity search, configured with cosine similarity as the distance metric across all experiments. It is used as a high-performance vector index for nearest neighbor search on dense sentence embeddings. In this implementation, the IndexFlatIP index is employed, which performs similarity search using the inner product (dot product). To enable cosine similarity search, sentence embeddings are normalized with L2 normalization before indexing, so that inner product similarity corresponds directly to cosine similarity. The FAISS index runs on CPU to enable compatibility with systems lacking GPU support, trading off some speed for broader accessibility and lower resource requirements. 3.2.2 Sentence Embedding Three different sentence embedding models generate dense vector representations of English sentences for retrieval• MiniLM: A compact transformer-based model producing 384-dimensional embeddings optimized for speed and efficiency. Generation Module The generation module utilizes the BLOOMZ-3B LLM [7], a multilingual, instruction-tuned variant of the BLOOM family with approximately 3 billion parameters. BLOOMZ-3B supports over 12 Indic languages, including Hindi and English, enabling robust cross-lingual generation tasks such as machine translation. The model architecture consists of 32 transformer layers, with a hidden size of 2560 and 20 attention heads, striking a balance between performance and computational efficiency. For translation, the model is prompted with a constructed input that includes the original English sentence along with examples retrieved from similar sentences, which helps the model produce more accurate and relevant translations. The decoding process uses parameters such as a temperature of 0.7 to control creativity and diversity, a maximum token length to limit output size, and padding with the model’s EOS token to properly terminate sequences. This setup facilitates effective and corresponding generation of Hindi translations from English inputs. 3.5. Evaluation Module Due to the inherent ambiguity and variability in language, multiple evaluation metrics were used to capture different facets of translation quality, including lexical, syntactic, and semantic accuracy. Metrics like BLEU, CHRF++, and METEOR (ranging from 0 to 100 for BLEU and CHRF++, and 0 to 1 for METEOR) focus mainly on lexical and syntactic overlap with the reference. COMET (ranging from -1 to 1) is a neural metric that relies on reference translations to evaluate the overall semantic adequacy and translation quality. In contrast, BERT Similarity (ranging from 0 to 1) leverages contextual embeddings to measure semantic closeness between the generated and reference sentences, capturing deeper meaning with less reliance on exact reference matching. 4. Conclusion and Future Scope Machine Translation remains an essential tool for bridging linguistic divides in multilingual societies like India. This study introduced a domain-specific English-to-Hindi translation framework using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with the BLOOMZ-3B language model. By employing FAISS-based dense retrieval and sentence encoders such as MiniLM, DistilUSE, and LaBSE, the system effectively retrieved contextually relevant examples to guide translation. Empirical evaluations across five diverse domains—Healthcare, Legal, Sports, Education, and News— revealed that the RAG-based approach consistently outperformed Zero-shot methods, particularly in semantic accuracy as reflected by higher BERT Similarity and COMET scores. While character-level metrics like BLEU and METEOR were slightly lower due to flexible paraphrasing, their impact on meaning retention was minimal. However, several limitations persist. Complex syntactic variations in morphologically rich Indic languages remain difficult to capture reliably. The selection and optimization of FAISS-based vector databases specific to Indic languages continues to pose a challenge, influencing both retrieval efficiency and quality. Additionally, the BLOOMZ model currently supports a limited subset of Indic languages, narrowing the system’s broader applicability. Related Works The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology in the health sector, especially for clinical decision-making, is rarely found in Indonesia. This is due to its questionable accuracy, lack of safety when implemented in real-world scenarios, also the fear of leaking patient privacy data [6] [7]. A study states that the use of AI in direct practice cannot be recommended when used independently without supervision from a doctor, although it performs quite well when working on theoretical medical exam questions [8]. Even so, there have been quite a few groups or individuals who have tried to create AI models specialized for medical tasks. One of them is MediTron, a set of open-source large language models (LLMs) designed specifically for medical use. MediTron is designed to improve lay people’s access to medical knowledge as well as support medical decision- making [9]. There are two main variants of this LLM, MediTron-7B and MediTron-70B, which are distinguished by the number of parameters, 7 billion and 70 billion respectively. The performance of MediTron-70B, which is built based on Meta’s Llama-2 model, is proven to be able to surpass models in its class such as ClinicalCamel-70B, Med42-70B, and even its own base model, Llama-2-70B [9]. To address the issue of inaccuracy and outdated of answers generated by LLM, a technique called Retrieval- Augmented Generation (RAG), which makes LLM capable of reading a PDF file, has been invented [10]. RAG accommodates several steps required by LLM in order to achieve the expected functionality, including external data search which is used to obtain information that has the same context [11]. Evaluation For evaluation, different sets of metrics have been combined together to identify the performance of both the proposed RAG and the standard language models. These metrics would grant a full-scale analysis regarding quality, accuracy, and semantic similarity of model outputs compared to the expected diagnoses. The evaluation is done on three models namely GPT-4o mini, Claude 3.5 Haiku, and Kesehatan-7B-v0.1, and 2 of those models, GPT-4o mini and Claude 3.5 Haiku applied with RAG. Kesehatan-7B-v0.1 is compared here as a representative of one of the Indonesian opensource models specifically trained using health data. These models will be evaluated and compared with these metrics: Precision, Recall, and F1-Score. These metrics are derived from a confusion matrix consisting of: • True Positive (TP): the model predicts the expected diagnosis correctly. • False Positive (FP): the model predicts a wrong diagnosis. • False Negative (FN): the model does not provide a diagnosis when an expected diagnosis exists. METEOR Score. METEOR (Metric for Evaluation of Translation with Explicit Ordering) score assesses lexical and semantic similarity between the model-generated outputs and the texts used as the reference. The score uses exact matches, synonyms, stems, alignment, and order [18]. 1738 Lenno Aubert Hartono et al. / Procedia Computer Science 269 (2025) 1732–1741 Precision, Recall, and F1-Score. These metrics are derived from a confusion matrix consisting of: • Precision (P): Proportion of matched unigrams in the candidate output relative to the total unigrams in the candidate • Recall (R): Proportion of matched unigrams relative to the total unigrams in the reference • Harmonic Mean (Fmean): Balances Precision and Recall with a weighted factor • Penalty: Penalizes the ”chunkiness” or misalignment of matched unigrams • METEOR Score: METEOR = Fmean · (1 − Penalty) (1) The purpose of METEOR is to evaluate the quality of generated outputs based on lexical matches, semantic meaning, and fluency. Limitations This research, however, is subject to several limitations. Limited development costs are one of them, where we have to find the cheapest solution in order to carry out this research within the budget range. Somaiya School of Engineering, Mumbai-400077, India Abstract Healthcare organizations face challenges in aligning audit-identified vulnerabilities with compliance frameworks like HIPAA and ISO 27001, a manual process that is error-prone and resource-intensive. This paper proposes a novel conceptual framework leveraging multi-modal Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) to automate this mapping and generate compliance-aligned remediation guidance. The system extracts vulnerabilities from audit reports (including text and visual elements), retrieves relevant regulatory controls semantically, and produces explainable recommendations to support regulatory adherence. In addition to automation, the framework addresses key deployment challenges such as data privacy risks, semantic mismatches, evolving regulations, and hallucination in AI outputs. Mitigation strategies include privacy-preserving techniques, explainable AI methods, and dynamic updates to the regulatory knowledge base. By unifying HIPAA and ISO 27001 within a scalable, multi-modal architecture, the proposed solution enhances patient data protection, with illustrative simulations showing potential 85% mapping accuracy and 70% reduction in manual effort, supporting sustainable, real-time compliance management. Introduction The healthcare sector faces escalating challenges in securing sensitive patient data amid rising cyberattacks and complex regulatory demands. Cyber threats targeting hospitals and digital health platforms threaten patient privacy and data integrity, while frequent security audits require organizations to demonstrate compliance with national and international standards [1, 2]. Manual processes for mapping audit-identified vulnerabilities to regulatory controls are slow, error-prone, and reliant on specialized expertise, often delaying remediation and increasing compliance risks [3, 4]. This paper proposes a novel conceptual framework using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to automate vulnerability mapping, enhancing compliance efficiency in healthcare. The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), a U.S. regulation, mandates safeguards for Protected Health Information (PHI), including encryption and access controls, with non-compliance risking penalties up to $1.5 million annually [5, 6]. ISO 27001, an international standard, provides a framework for an Information Security Management System (ISMS), emphasizing risk-based security across industries [7, 8]. For healthcare organizations, aligning audit findings with both frameworks is critical for regulatory certification and risk management. Mapping HIPAA’s PHI-specific controls to ISO 27001’s broader ISMS principles enables unified compliance strategies, but manual efforts remain labor-intensive and prone to inconsistencies [9]. Fig. 1. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a hybrid AI paradigm that combines semantic retrieval with generative capabilities, ideal for processing complex regulatory texts [10, 11]. As shown in Figure 1 RAG consists of a retriever, which identifies relevant documents from a knowledge base, and a generator, which produces contextually accurate outputs, reducing errors common in traditional systems [12, 13]. In healthcare, RAG’s ability to handle extensive compliance makes it suitable for automating control mapping, improving accuracy and traceability [14, 15]. Although retrievalaugmented generation (RAG) effectively mitigates these issues by incorporating external knowledge, traditional approaches are primarily limited to textual data, failing to leverage the rich multimodal nature of clinical information, which potentially compromises diagnostic accuracy. Multimodal RAG extends information processing capabilities to encompass diverse data types, thus overcoming the limitations of its text-only counterpart. Introduction In recent years, with the rapid advancement of AI and natural language processing (NLP) technologies, their applications in the medical domain have become increasingly diverse. The introduction of the Transformer architecture [1] and the subsequent emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) have further accelerated the integration of AI into medical practice and research. With their robust capabilities in language understanding and generation, LLMs have demonstrated immense potential for application across various facets of the medical field. For instance, LLMs are capable of assisting in the identification of potential diseases by analyzing data such as patient symptoms and medical records and providing evidence-based recommendations for clinical decision-making through the analysis of extensive medical data [2]. LLMs can also automatically generate clinical notes and discharge summaries or extract key information from lengthy clinician-patient dialogues to produce medical summaries, thereby alleviating the documentation burden on clinicians [3]. Furthermore, LLMs can serve as powerful assistants in medical research by rapidly reviewing large volumes of literature, generating abstracts, and aiding in literature screening, thus significantly enhancing research efficiency [4].

Relying on static training data, the parametric knowledge of LLMs remains frozen once training is complete. Furthermore, functioning as black-box models, LLMs often lack transparency and interpretability in their reasoning processes [7]. This consequently hinders users from effectively assessing the reliability of generated content, thereby impeding the models’ deeper integration into clinical decision-making. To address the above issues, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has been introduced as an effective strategy. RAG is a paradigm that integrates generative models with external databases. Before generating a response, a retriever first identifies relevant document fragments from external knowledge sources based on the input; subsequently, a generator concatenates this retrieved information with the original input, utilizing it as enriched context to guide the generation process [8]. Its primary advantage lies in the ability to synergistically combine the intrinsic knowledge of LLMs with vast, dynamic external knowledge bases. By outputting content based on retrieved external knowledge and providing traceable references, RAG reduces factual inaccuracies and enhances the verifiability and overall trustworthiness of the responses. Fundamental principles of RAG The foundational paradigm of RAG, as proposed by Lewis et al. [8], combines parametric and non-parametric memory. Parametric memory is embodied by a pre-trained LLM, where all knowledge learned during training—including linguistic patterns, factual information, and reasoning abilities—is stored within its neural network weights. This knowledge is inherent and static, and updating it requires a costly retraining process. Non-parametric memory, on the other hand, consists of an external, easily accessible knowledge base that is simple to update. This memory is accessed through a dedicated retriever. The RAG workflow typically follows a "retrieve-then-read" pattern. When a user poses a query, the retriever first identifies the most relevant information snippets from the non-parametric knowledge base. This retrieved information, along with the original query, is then supplied as an augmented prompt to the parametric generator. Subsequently, the generator synthesizes the final answer based on this real-time, verifiable information. 2.1.1. The retrieval module The retrieval module is the information acquisition engine of a RAG system. Its core task is to efficiently and accurately locate the most relevant information snippets from a vast knowledge base based on the user’s query. The quality of retrieval directly determines the quality of the context available to the generator, thereby influencing the accuracy of the final answer. Sparse retrieval excels at handling queries containing specific technical terms, abbreviations, or entity names but has limited capabilities in understanding conceptual or synonymous queries. Dense retrieval typically utilizes encoder models (e.g., BERT [16]) to encode queries and document chunks into embeddings within the same vector space. The retrieval process is then completed by calculating the similarity between the query and document vectors. The core advantage of dense retrieval lies in its ability to capture semantic meaning, allowing for successful matches even when the query and document do not share keywords, as long as their meanings are similar [17]. However, the upper bound of its effectiveness is limited by the knowledge contained within the pre-trained retriever model itself. To combine the semantic understanding of dense retrieval with the lexical precision of sparse retrieval, hybrid search emerged. It executes both dense and sparse retrieval simultaneously, then merges and re-ranks the results using a weighted fusion strategy. This method effectively balances the needs for semantic understanding and precise keyword matching, making it suitable for scenarios that require both interpreting user intent and accurately retrieving proper nouns [18]. Traditional RAG performs retrieval only once before generation begins, which is inadequate for long-form generation tasks that require continuous information. The FLARE framework, proposed by Jiang et al. [19], transforms retrieval into an active, iterative process. It first generates a temporary future sentence and then checks for the presence of low-confidence tokens. If such tokens exist, FLARE uses this predicted future content as a query to retrieve additional relevant information and then regenerates the sentence with this new information. This on-demand retrieval strategy avoids unnecessary information acquisition, making the generation process more dynamic and factually reliable. Traditional RAG typically retrieves isolated text chunks, which limits a holistic understanding of the overall context of long documents. The RAPTOR model, proposed by Sarthi et al. Methods for multimodal data fusion In modern clinical practice, the decision-making process is inherently multimodal, potentially integrating information from various sources such as radiological images, EHRs, pathology reports, physiological signals, and genomic sequences. Developing AI systems capable of integrating and understanding these heterogeneous data streams is crucial, and multimodal representation learning forms the technical cornerstone of such systems. To navigate these techniques effectively, it is essential to explicitly distinguish between two foundational concepts: fusion and alignment. Specifically, fusion describes when information from different modalities is combined within a model’s architecture (e.g., at early, intermediate, or late stages). In contrast, alignment (discussed in Section 2.2.2) refers to how different modalities are mapped into a comparable semantic space to enable cross-modal understanding. Focusing first on fusion, methods are generally categorized based on the architectural stage of integration. Early fusion, also known as feature-level fusion, is centered on the idea of merging raw data or shallow features from different modalities at the initial stages of model training to form a unified feature vector. This vector is then fed into a single downstream model for processing. Common techniques for achieving this fusion include simple feature concatenation, pooling, or the use of gated units [25]. The primary advantage of early fusion is its ability to capture correlations and interactions between low-level features of different modalities early in the network. However, it can suffer from the modality gap and is prone to creating extremely high-dimensional features after concatenation, leading to the curse of dimensionality. Metrics for generation tasks Common text metrics: BLEU- This metric was initially proposed for machine translation, evaluating text quality by computing n-gram precision between candidate texts and reference texts, supplemented by a brevity penalty [159]. The metric is simple to compute, language-independent, and therefore widely used in natural language generation tasks. However, BLEU shows poor correlation with human judgments at the sentence level and, due to its reliance on literal word matching, struggles to effectively capture semantic similarity. ROUGE- A set of metrics for automatically evaluating the quality of a summary by comparing it with ideal summaries created by humans. Unlike the precision-based BLEU, the core of ROUGE is recall. Among its variants, ROUGE-N measures the degree of overlap by calculating the recall of n-grams between the candidate and reference summaries, while ROUGE-L measures the longest common subsequence to better capture sentence-level structure by rewarding in-sequence word matches [160]. However, this metric is still limited by its reliance on surface-level lexical overlap. METEOR- This metric is based on unigram alignment between the candidate and reference texts. It matches not only exact words but also word variants and synonyms through stemming and external knowledge bases like WordNet. METEOR combines unigram precision and recall and introduces a fragmentation penalty, which is calculated based on the number of matched chunks to reward more fluently ordered sentences. METEOR generally shows a higher correlation with human judgments than BLEU [161]. It calculates precision, recall, and F1 scores based on the cosine similarity between token embeddings in the candidate and reference texts. The prevailing strategy to address this issue is learning a shared latent embedding space. Due to its high sensitivity, medical data is often isolated within individual healthcare institutions, creating data silos. Federated learning (FL) offers an innovative solution to this dilemma. It is a distributed, privacy-preserving machine learning framework. In a typical FL process, a global model is distributed to participating institutions (e.g., hospitals), each of which trains the model on its local, private data. Afterward, updated model parameters (such as gradients) are sent back anonymously to a central server for aggregation, which in turn updates the global model [186]. The assessment benchmark relies on the Medical Licensure Examination’s rich question bank, which compre­ hensively covers the three major exam areas, including Basic Medical Theory, Clinical Medicine, and 16 core exam subjects, totaling 9788 questions and 5473 practice questions. The data includes 2 core tasks, (1) Medical knowledge comprehension assessment: based on the given questions, select the correct candidate answers and give the corre­ sponding parses. (2) Medical semantic reasoning assessment: based on the given premises and assumptions, determine the relationship be­ tween them. 4.1.1. Medical knowledge understanding task Firstly, the text-based exercises in PDF format are cleaned, and using custom rules, the questions, options, correct answers, subjects, and standard explanations are extracted. This information is then converted into a structured JSON format. It includes three types of questions, as shown in Table 3. For A1/A2-type questions, the model’s input is the content of the "question," and the output includes both the "answer" and the "analysis". For A3-type questions, each stem corresponds to a list of questions, consisting of multiple sub-questions. The model’s input includes the shared stem, the sub-question, and the output of the previous sub- question. The target output is the "answer" and the "analysis" for each sub-question. For B1-type questions, each shared set of options corre­ sponds to a list of questions, consisting of multiple sub-questions. The model’s input includes the shared options, the sub-question, and the output of the previous sub-question. The target output is the "answer" and the "analysis" for each sub-question. To accommodate the different types of questions, separate instruction templates are constructed, which include a task description, a reasoning chain, and restrictions on the question-answer format. The task description clarifies how to approach each question type, while the reasoning chain is designed to guide the large language model in selecting an option and simultaneously providing the corresponding explanation. 4.1.2. Medical semantic reasoning task The data for Task 2 comes from the Tianchi Traditional Chinese Medicine AI Special Competition, and the data link is https://tianchi. aliyun.com/competition/entrance/532199/information. In the research, a total of 29,497 Natural Language Inference (NLI) data pairs were constructed. The hypothesis is that if there is stable semantic similarity between two sentences, it should be possible to infer the hy­ pothesis from the premise and vice versa. Given the significant length differences between the problem answers and the standard explana­ tions, half of the data pairs in NLI have undergone premise and hy­ pothesis swapping to eliminate any bias caused by length. The model’s input consists of the “premise" and "hypothesis,” and the output is the “label”. Thus, the task involves inputting the premise and hypothesis, and outputting the corresponding label. The sample data for Task 2 is as follows: { “idx”: 0. “premise”: “Clinical infection, also known as symptomatic infection, refers to the invasion of pathogens into the human body, which not only triggers an immune response but also leads to tissue damage and pathological changes through the action of the pathogens themselves or the body’s hypersensitivity reactions. Option A pertains to the clearance of pathogens. Option B pertains to asymptomatic infection. Option D pertains to latent infection. Option E pertains to the carrier state of pathogens.”, “hypothesis”: “Medical care institutions must strictly implement disinfection and isolation protocols in accordance with the relevant regulations of the State Council’s health administrative department to prevent hospital-acquired infections and iatrogenic infections.”, “label”: 2 } The label values are 0 and 2, where 0 indicates that there is an entailment relationship between the premise and the hypothesis, and 2 indicates that the premise and the hypothesis are unrelated or contradictory. 4.2. Conclusion Based on over 15,000 sample data entries from the Medical Knowl­ edge Understanding and Reasoning Ability Evaluation Competition, our research focuses on the tasks of medical knowledge understanding and medical semantic reasoning. Using Qwen-14 B-Chat as the base model, we propose an improved retrieval-augmented generative modeling al­ gorithm. The main improvements include data processing, prompt selection, and the fusion of dense and sparse retrievers. Compared to four large base models, the average comprehensive evaluation metrics have increased by +3.86 %, verifying the effectiveness of our method. Additionally, ablation experiments demonstrate that each improvement enhances the base model. However, this study still has limitations: firstly, the data originates from a competition, and its domain coverage may not fully represent the real-world clinical diversity. secondly, evaluation mainly relies on standard metrics, lacking in-depth exploration of the model’s perfor­ mance in actual clinical environments. In the future, we plan to explore several key directions: expanding data sources by incorporating diverse real clinical case to enhance the model’s generalization and under­ standing of rare diseases. Developing more explainable versions to improve transparency and foster trust among doctors. Integrating the method into clinical decision support systems and intelligent consulta­ tion platforms to optimize the model through practical feedback, and investigating its potential value in areas like medical education and auxiliary diagnosis.
